Our fibre/Fourier test (see #273, knowledge/reductions/273/) transfers to #7 verbatim - every divisor m>1 of odd L is admissible, the reciprocal screen becomes 'L is ODD ABUNDANT' (smallest 945), and the condition collapses to: max over n|L, n<L of (2n - sigma(n)) <= sigma(L) - 2L. It eliminates 191 of the 391 candidates below 200,000 (including 945: 58 > 30 at n=189) and gives a floor of 3,465. Prizes: Erdos $25 for nonexistence, Selfridge $2000 for an explicit example.

rationale: Statement disambiguation: the site's bare wording omits 'distinct'. Erdos-Graham [ErGr80] and google-deepmind/formal-conjectures (StrictCoveringSystem, injective_moduli) both require DISTINCT moduli; without that the problem is trivially YES (0,1,2,3 mod 4, and 4=5-1). Any formalisation without injective moduli is unfaithful.

Parity reduction (self-derived, verified numerically): every allowed modulus p-1 is even, so a congruence class with even residue lies wholly in the evens and one with odd residue wholly in the odds. Halving turns the problem into: find TWO DISJOINT distinct-modulus covering systems with moduli drawn from H = {m>=2 : 2m+1 prime}.

Self-verified lcm floor: if L' is the lcm of the halved moduli then f(L') = sum over d|L', 2d+1 prime, of 1/d must be >= 2 (each of the two disjoint families needs reciprocal sum >= 1). A divisor sieve to 3e6 gives min{L' : f(L') >= 2} = 27720, so the lcm of the original moduli is at least 55440, and only 29 candidate values of L' are <= 200000.

Exhaustive elimination of the 29 candidate lcms below 200000 by DFS (residues forced by covering the least uncovered point, pruned on combined remaining density vs unused reciprocal budget) is INCONCLUSIVE: the tree exceeds 3e6 nodes per candidate. Neither found nor eliminated by this route.

Constructive search is not close. Randomized reciprocal-balanced splits of the divisor pool followed by a greedy ascending build, on the three richest candidates (L'=3603600/2162160/3243240, budgets 2.30/2.29/2.28, 230-343 restarts each), leave 11.7-12.3 percent of the two cyclic groups uncovered at best. A SINGLE covering system from H is easy to build greedily; the obstruction is entirely the disjointness, because the density sits in the small moduli 2,3,5,6,8,9,11 that only one of the two families can hold.

Open, and both directions resist. The parity reduction (all moduli p-1 are even, so residues split by parity) makes it exactly TWO DISJOINT covering systems with distinct moduli drawn from H={m>=2 : 2m+1 prime}; the reciprocal budget over any smooth lcm below 4e6 tops out at 2.30, leaving ~0.15 slack per system, so a witness is cramped but not excluded. A harness run reached only lcm<=55439, which is one below the first numerically viable candidate (55440=2*27720) - i.e. it stopped exactly where the search starts being hard.

stage_reduce found and CHECKED three structural reductions, two of them new to us: (a) the parity decomposition - all moduli p-1 are even, so a solution is exactly TWO covering systems with disjoint moduli drawn from H2={(p-1)/2}; (b) no admissible modulus is 2 mod 6, since m=2 mod 3 forces 3|p, so 8,14,20,26,... are excluded and the standard 2,4,8,16 doubling chain is blocked at its second step; (c) any solution needs at least 18 congruences, because the 17 smallest elements of H2 have reciprocal sum 1.99835 < 2, which also gives a mid-search rejection filter (sum of 2/m must reach 2, not sum of 1/m reach 1).

CORRECTION (2026-09-11): previously scored 6, below #677's 7, which contradicted the assessment. On the axis score actually measures - is a COMPLETE proof mechanically reachable - #273 is the stronger of the two: its affirmative side is a finite certificate at a reachable size (29 candidate lcms up to 393120), so a solver returning SAT at any one of them resolves the problem outright. #677 has no reachable route in either direction. The earlier 6-vs-7 reflected #677's already-banked partial value, which belongs on the partial axis, not this one.

Candidate ordering matters more than candidate size. slack(L) = sum of 1/m over admissible divisors minus 1 bounds the unused reciprocal weight, so every modulus with 1/m > slack is FORCED. L=55440 is the smallest of the 29 candidates but among the loosest (slack 0.0437, only 7 of 43 forced); three attempts were spent on it for that reason alone. L=100800 is the uniquely collapsible one: slack 0.000089, 45 of 50 forced, 5 free, overlap budget 9 points, and only 12 of 32 free subsets reach coverage. Two of those 12 have overlap exactly 0 and are excluded by Mirsky-Newman/Davenport-Rado (a disjoint covering system must repeat its largest modulus, so distinct moduli admit no exact cover) - the first cases on this problem eliminated by a theorem rather than a timer.

The generating-function condition is now derived and validated, not a hunch. For every divisibility-maximal modulus m in the chosen set, L/m <= overlap - because at a primitive m-th root of unity only that term has a pole, giving |sum over the excess multiset of zeta^r| = L/m exactly. Checked to 1e-15 on a known cover with two maximal moduli. It subsumes Mirsky-Newman (overlap 0 demands L/m <= 0) and cuts L=100800's 12 coverage-reaching subsets to 7 in milliseconds, where a SAT encoding of ONE subset did not decide in 37 minutes. Standard argument, no novelty claimed.

FIBRE/FOURIER ELIMINATION (2026-09-11, $0, no model calls): for every d|L and primitive d-th root of unity zeta, sum over m in U with d|m of (L/m)zeta^{a_m} equals the zeta-transform of the excess, so its modulus is at most k = sum L/m - L. Reverse triangle inequality gives a residue-free screen 2*max(W)-sum(W) > k. This ELIMINATES 20 of the 29 candidate lcm values below 400000, including BOTH candidates that consumed every previous attempt: L=55440 (three attempts, margin 2437 vs k<=2421) and L=100800 (two attempts, 1903 vs k<=9). Four solver runs timed out on those two; the test decides both in under a millisecond.

Search floor advances from a SCREEN at 55440 to EXHAUSTIVE at 110880 - every candidate below that is now excluded by proof. Surviving candidates below 400000: 110880, 166320, 221760, 262080, 277200, 302400, 332640, 388080, 393120, all loose (slack 0.02-0.08, k in the thousands) where the inequality has no bite. The 400000 cap is compute, not a theorem.

The test bites hardest exactly where a candidate looks most attractive: k <= slack*L, so the tiny-slack candidates chosen for being nearly determined have almost no excess budget. m=16 does most of the work (17 prime, so 16 is admissible and forced) while the other admissible multiples of 16 are too sparse to cancel its weight. Standard Mirsky-Newman style argument applied at every d rather than only the largest modulus; no novelty of technique claimed.

FOLLOW-UP (2026-09-11): the fibre/Fourier family is now provably EXHAUSTED, by decision rather than by search. Every d-constraint is implied by the constraint at mu = min{m in U : d|m}, so the family collapses to: for every mu in U, L/mu - sum_{m in U, mu|m, m!=mu} L/m <= k_U. That form is monotone in U, so a mu violating it under the maximal admissible set violates under every subset containing it and can be deleted outright; iterating to a fixed point is COMPLETE in polynomial time. No 2^47 enumeration is needed.

Propagation eliminates exactly the same 20 candidates and deletes ZERO moduli at all nine survivors - the full admissible set already satisfies every constraint there, so no subset search can improve on it. The survivors fall short by 1944 to 19326; the closest, L=302400, misses by 1944 against a budget of 6700 (a 29 percent gap), versus 55440 which is over by only 16. Regression: 3130 genuine covering systems built across L=12..720, zero false kills.

The reason is intrinsic: k <= slack*L, so the inequality bites exactly when slack is tiny. The 20 eliminated are the tight candidates; the nine survivors all have slack 0.02-0.08 and thousands of units of excess to absorb any imbalance. Tightness is both what makes a candidate look attackable AND what this test needs, so the algebra consumed exactly the candidates a search would have preferred and left the ones that are loose for both.

Do not spend solver time on L=55440 or L=100800; both are eliminated by algebra. Run the fibre/Fourier screen at every d BEFORE any SAT encoding - it is free and it killed 20 of 29 candidates that four solver runs could not.

The nine surviving candidates need a genuinely different lever: the residue-free bound has no bite when slack is large. Either strengthen to an exact minimum over d-th roots of unity, combine several d simultaneously, or encode those nine for SAT.

Do not attempt subset branch-and-bound on the nine survivors: the propagation decision is complete and returns nothing. The thread identifies the problem as equivalent to R^r_{r-1}(K_{r+1}) <= r^2+1, a named quantity in the weakened-Ramsey and complementary-Ramsey literatures (Chung-Liu 1978 Theorem 3.6 gives R^3_2(K_4,K_4,K_4)=10, i.e. the r=3 case, 21 years before [ErGy99]; Harborth-Moller 1999; Munemasa-Shinohara). Equality holds whenever the affine plane of order r exists - which for r=10 it does NOT (Lam-Thiel-Swiercz), so r=10 may behave differently from the prime-power ladder.

rationale: Quantifier reading: formal-conjectures states this as forall m n k, k>0 -> m >= n+k -> lcmInterval m k != lcmInterval n k. The two solutions Erdos knew (M(4,3)=M(13,2), M(3,4)=M(19,2)) use l != k and are NOT counterexamples to this statement.
Self-verified counterexample floor: exhaustive same-k scan found no (n,k,m) with m >= n+k and M(n,k)=M(m,k) for n,m < 4e5 (k<=3), < 2e5 (k<=6) and < 8e4 (7<=k<=20).

Structural finding from the same scan: same-k lcm collisions DO occur, but every one found has OVERLAPPING intervals with a tiny gap - max m-n observed is 1 (k=3,4,5,7), 2 (k=6,8), 3 (k=10,12,16), 4 (k=20) - against the m-n >= k the conjecture needs, and all of them sit at small n (n <= 16). So the negative direction has no cheap witness and a bounded search is close to futile.

Bounded-divisor reduction (this session, rigorous): d_k(n) = P_k(n)/M(n,k) is PERIODIC in n with period dividing prod_{p<=k} p^{floor(log_p(k-1))+1} (12, 36, 360, 1800, 12600, 88200, 176400 for k=3..9), verified over three periods each, so its value set is exhaustive. Hence M(n,k)=M(m,k) forces P_k(m)/P_k(n) = d_k(m)/d_k(n), a ratio from an explicit finite list.
PROVED for k=1 and k=2: d_k is identically 1 there, so M(n,k)=P_k(n) is strictly increasing and m>n already gives M(m,k)!=M(n,k). These are the two lemmas most worth certifying in Lean.

Because the ratio list is exhaustive, sweeping n rules out EVERY m (unbounded), not just m in a window: no counterexample for k=3 or k=4 with n < 1e8, k=5 or k=6 with n < 1e6, k=7 or k=8 with n < 2e5. For k=3 the whole question is the single equation (x-1)x(x+1)=2(y-1)y(y+1), whose only solution with x>y below 1e8 is (5,4) = the overlapping pair (n,m)=(2,3).

Smoothness obstruction: if M(n,k)=M(m,k) with m>=n+k then every prime p>k dividing any of m+1..m+k satisfies p <= (m-n)+(k-1), because p divides some n+i and m+j>n+i. So all of m+1..m+k are max(k, m-n+k-1)-smooth.

Open. The negative direction (find n,k,m with m>=n+k and lcm(n+1..n+k)=lcm(m+1..m+k)) is a finite certificate but no counterexample exists in any reachable range: verified none for k<=12 with n,m<=2e5, and k=3 reduces to the single cubic x^3-x=2(y^3-y), exhaustive to y<1e9 with only the degenerate y=4,x=5 (that is n=2,m=3, where m-n=1<k, which the hypothesis allows). The positive direction is Erdos's conjecture and needs new mathematics: k<=2 is elementary, k=3 is already a Thue-Siegel/elliptic-type Diophantine problem.

rationale: AlphaProof proved J(18,9) != 10 and that proof is in a PR to formal-conjectures; the problem reduces to Johnson-graph chromatic numbers, with k=4 known via chi(J(6,3))=6.

Equivalent to asking whether chi(J(2k,k)) = k+1 for some k>2 (Johnson graph). Published chromatic-number tables already settle 3<=k<=8 NEGATIVELY, and Ma-Tang proved chi > k+1 for every k>2 not of the form p-1 with p prime. So the open frontier is k in {10,12,16,18,22,...}, and the smallest, k=10, is a chromatic-number question on J(20,10) with 184,756 vertices and 167,960 rainbow constraints - not a small SAT instance. The 'finite example' label is real but the reachable cases are all decided.

For the 'or forest' half, Hoggar's theorem means a forest can only fail if a tree component is already non-log-concave, and the smallest such tree has 26 vertices (Kadrawi-Levit).
